findings.title: Denial cache key concatenates name and folder with '_' and can collide
findings.body: userPermDenialCacheKey joins userUID, action, name and parent with unescaped '_' separators. Grafana resource UIDs can contain underscores (the tests themselves use UIDs like 'some_dashboard' and 'some_folder_parent'). Dashboard 'a_b' in folder 'c' and dashboard 'a' in folder 'b_c' both produce the key '...perm_<uid>_<action>_a_b_c'. Check consults the denial cache before any permission lookup and returns deny on a hit (service.go lines 116-121), so a denial recorded for one resource causes a false deny for the other for up to the 30s TTL, even when the user has access to it. The key needs an unambiguous encoding (a delimiter that cannot appear in UIDs, or a hash of a structured tuple).

findings.title: Cached denial is checked first and never invalidated, so it can keep blocking a just-created resource
findings.body: The denial cache is consulted before cached or DB permissions and is only cleared by TTL (30s). The PR's fix for newly created resources is the DB fallback on a permission-cache miss, but that fallback is bypassed whenever the same (user, action, name, folder) was denied within the last 30s. A plausible sequence: a client checks access to a dashboard UID before it exists (authz runs before the storage lookup), gets Allowed=false, and that denial is written at lines 153-155. After the dashboard is created and the creator's permission is written, the creator's check for the same name/folder still returns false until the entry expires. The same staleness applies to any later grant of access. Denials should not short-circuit fresher permission data, or they should be invalidated on create/permission changes.

findings.title: DB fallback re-reads permissions but still uses the cached folder tree
findings.body: When the permission cache misses, Check calls getIdentityPermissions and then checkPermission, which reaches checkInheritedPermissions and buildFolderTree (called at line 590). buildFolderTree returns the folderCache entry (TTL 30s) if present (this line). A subfolder created after the tree was cached is absent from that tree, so Ancestors() does not walk through it and grants inherited from its parent folder are not found. Dashboards in the new subfolder are then denied for up to 30s, even though this fallback was added precisely so newly created resources are picked up. The fallback only refreshes the permission map, not the folder data it depends on.

findings.title: Every denied check missing the permission cache now queries the DB
findings.body: Before this change, a denied check with a warm permission cache returned without touching the DB, since getUserPermissions read permCache first. Now, when the cached map does not contain the resource, Check always falls through to getIdentityPermissions (line 139), which runs the full permissionStore.GetUserPermissions query for the action. The 30s denial cache only suppresses repeats for the same (name, folder). Each distinct resource a user is denied on, such as a client probing many UIDs or a user hitting resources they cannot access, therefore produces a full permission query, and sequential checks are not coalesced by singleflight. DB load now scales with the number of distinct denied resources. The fallback should be rate-limited or coalesced per user/action, or the cost should be accepted explicitly.

findings.title: Denial-precedence test sets the permission cache to false, so it does not exercise the denial cache
findings.body: The test 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' says the permission cache entry allows access 'to prove this is not checked', but the value is false, so the cached permission path also denies. The DB fallback (fakeStore with no userPermissions) also returns nothing, so the request is denied even if the permDenialCache lookup in Check were removed. The assertion assert.False therefore passes without the new code path. Setting the permission cache value to true would make the test fail unless the denial entry takes precedence, which is what the test is meant to guard.
